description: Desarrollando una solución integral para el desafío del Mapa de Marte en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Combinamos ingeniería de software, visualización geoespacial y análisis de datos científicos para construir una herramienta táctica y multicapa. Nuestro objetivo es transformar datos complejos de misiones de la NASA en un sistema interactivo que guíe y proteja a los astronautas en futuras caminatas marcianas.
summary:
We developed Martian Map, a web-based EVA planner that helps future astronauts explore Mars safely. It runs on an interactive 3D globe and focuses on Gale crater (Mount Sharp), where NASA's Curiosity rover operates today.

The challenge asks for a map that guides human survival and exploration on Mars. Martian Map answers it by turning real NASA and USGS data into walking routes: an A* algorithm computes paths over the USGS 1-meter elevation model that avoid dangerous slopes. Users choose a science mission and a route profile, and see the route's distance, elevation profile and slopes, a terrain slope map, and the real sites Curiosity drilled, with their minerals and photos. During the simulated walk, suit telemetry combines real Curiosity data (temperature, pressure, radiation) with an oxygen model that orders a turnaround when needed.

This matters because the first human missions will have limited oxygen and time. Martian Map shows how existing Mars data can support safer, science-driven decisions before astronauts ever set foot there.
details:
Martian Map is an EVA (extravehicular activity) planner for future astronauts on Mars. It computes safe walking routes over the real terrain of Gale crater (Mount Sharp), where the Curiosity rover is operating today, and displays them on a 3D globe.

How it works
The user selects a science mission (the “boxwork” ridges at Nevado Sajama or the crystal block at the Nazca site), an EVA start time, and a route profile (direct, low slope, or conservative). An A* algorithm finds the safest path over the USGS 1 m digital elevation model and shows:

  • route distance, elevation gain/loss and slopes, with an elevation profile;
  • a terrain slope map (from flat to hazardous);
  • the real sites where Curiosity drilled, with their minerals and NASA photos.

During the traverse, the suit telemetry combines real Curiosity data (temperature, pressure and radiation) with a model of oxygen, heart rate and battery. If the oxygen is not enough to return, the app orders a turnaround.

Formulas

  1. Slope of each cell (Horn 3×3 operator on the 1 m DEM):
    dz/dx = [(z3 + 2·z6 + z9) − (z1 + 2·z4 + z7)] / (8·Δx)
    dz/dy = [(z7 + 2·z8 + z9) − (z1 + 2·z2 + z3)] / (8·Δy)
    slope = arctan( √( (dz/dx)² + (dz/dy)² ) )
  2. Cost of moving between two cells (A*):
    cost = d · [1 + Ws·(mean slope / 15°)² + Wh·hazard + Wu·uncertainty] + We·|Δelevation|
    d = distance in meters. Weights per profile: Direct (all 0), Low slope (Ws = 10), Conservative (Ws = 10, Wh = 8, Wu = 6, We = 0.10).
  3. A* heuristic: h = straight-line distance to the goal, √(Δx² + Δy²), which guarantees the lowest-cost route.
  4. Walking time: t = distance / speed (2 km/h).
  5. Oxygen (SIM model):
    consumption = 1 + load (kg) / 50 → with 23 kg of equipment, O₂ is used 1.46× faster
    O₂ needed = round-trip time × consumption (must be ≤ the 6 h EVA limit)
    turnaround point = EVA limit / (2 × consumption)
  6. Heart rate (SIM): bpm = 85 + 1.5 × load (kg).
  7. Battery (SIM): 10 %/h, plus 6 %/h extra when the temperature is below −40 °C.
  8. Temperature by time of day (REMS data: 0 °C max, −70 °C min):
    T(h) = −35 + 35 · cos( 2π · (h − 14) / 24 ) → peak at 14:00
  9. Accumulated radiation (RAD data: 0.67 mSv/day): dose = 0.67 / 24 × EVA hours.

Benefits and impact
It turns complex scientific data into clear decisions: where to walk, how long it takes, and whether it is safe. It shows how existing orbiter and rover data can be used to plan the first human missions, balancing science and safety. It is also an educational tool about the real terrain of Mars.

Creativity
It is a complete mission simulation: the astronaut leaves the habitat at Bradbury Landing (where Curiosity landed), walks over the real terrain meter by meter and, on arrival, sees the real photo of the site and the minerals Curiosity found there.

Tools

  • Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, CesiumJS and Cesium Ion (3D Mars globe).
  • Backend: Python 3.14, FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, Pydantic, uv and pytest; custom A* algorithm.
  • Data: USGS (Gale 1 m DEM), NASA/JPL-Caltech (Curiosity positions and photos), and Curiosity’s REMS and RAD instruments.
  • Development: Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub (branches and pull requests), Docker and Render (web deployment).
  • An AI assistant (Claude) supported programming and writing; the design, data and integration were done by the team.

Factors considered

  • Safety: slope limits and enough oxygen to go and come back.
  • Transparency: every value is labeled as real data (USGS, REMS, RAD) or simulated (SIM).
  • Usability: a clear interface that adapts to phones, tablets and computers.

Limitations

  • It only covers an area of about 0.7 × 1.3 km with 1 m data; it cannot detect rocks or sand smaller than one meter.
  • Routes are based on slope only; hazard layers are not included yet.
  • Suit telemetry is simulated, and environmental data are averages, not real-time.
  • It is a prototype: it has not been validated by mission operations experts, and the free hosting may be slow on the first load.
